subject: Private hosting model: FQDN ownership, proxy cert handshake, and trust model decision

Subject: Redwood private deploy - FQDN ownership and TLS options

Hi Sofia,

Thanks again for the demo this week. We're close to a formal security review for the private deployment option. Two items SecOps asked us to confirm before we proceed:

1) FQDN ownership model for tenant endpoints. Acme wants clarity on what hostnames Redwood expects to own vs which must be delegated to our DNS (split-horizon or CNAME-based).

2) TLS termination model: do you recommend an internal TLS proxy (Redwood-managed certs on edge) or a CSR-proxy pattern where Acme's PKI issues certs for the backend, and Redwood performs pass-through with mTLS to the runtime?

I've attached a rough network sketch and a sample CSR we were given earlier. Can your team outline the trust model options and the operational expectations (cert rotation, revocation, auditing)?

Best,
Patrick

From: sofia_ivanova <sofia_ivanova@redwood.ai>
To: Patrick Harris <patrick.harris@acmeanalytics.com>
Cc: jonas_weber <jonas_weber@redwood.ai>, karthik_iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.ai>

Subject: Re: Redwood private deploy - FQDN ownership and TLS options

Patrick — thanks for the clear ask and the sketch. Looping in Jonas and Karthik to surface the operational tradeoffs. Below is a short summary of three practical models we've used on past private deployments; I'll call out pros/cons and what we need from Acme to operate each.

Model A — Delegated FQDN + Redwood edge certs (Redwood-managed TLS proxy)- What it looks like: Acme creates a CNAME or delegates a subdomain (e.g., *.redwood-acme.internal) to a Redwood-managed edge hostname. Redwood terminates TLS at the edge and forwards to the private runtime over the internal network.- Pros: simplest for Acme; Redwood handles cert lifecycle and public CA trust; easy canarying and rollout.- Cons: requires Acme to delegate DNS for the served FQDNs or provide CNAMEs; Acme trusting Redwood with plaintext termination at edge unless mTLS is used to backend.- Operational ask: DNS delegation/CNAMEs, an allowlist for Redwood edge IPs, and a contact for emergency cert rotation.

Model B — Split-horizon DNS + internal TLS pass-through (Customer certs at origin)- What it looks like: Public-facing FQDN resolves to Acme-controlled frontdoors. Within Acme VPC, FQDN resolves to Redwood private endpoints. TLS is terminated at the origin inside Acme (customer-managed certs). Redwood proxies are TCP-level; we rely on mTLS (mutual TLS) between Redwood runtime and Acme origin for authentication.- Pros: Acme retains end-to-end TLS ownership and can enforce PKI policies.- Cons: more operational work for Acme to manage certs and ensure rotations; split-horizon DNS complexity; failover to hosted variants is more complex.- Operational ask: a small service account for cert upload/validation OR automated CSR flow, documented rotation windows, and an audit log endpoint to push revocation events.

Model C — CSR-proxy / hybrid (Redwood presents boundary certs, origin certs validated by Redwood)- What it looks like: Acme signs a CA or issues origin certs; Redwood accepts CSRs signed by Acme and caches origin cert assertions. Edge terminates TLS with Redwood certs but validates origin certs and enforces pinning (short lived). Can be coupled with mTLS to backend.- Pros: balances operational load; Acme retains PKI authority while Redwood enables standard edge features (caching, WAF, canary).- Cons: operational complexity in handshake and validation; requires initial CA trust exchange and periodic revalidation.- Operational ask: initial CA bundle provisioned to Redwood (via secure transfer), CSR endpoint contract for rotation, and defined CRL/OCSP workflow.

Next steps from Redwood's side: Jonas, can you add a short checklist for each model (DNS requirements, cert formats, monitoring hooks, and failure modes)? Karthik, please confirm whether our private runtime supports mTLS mutual auth to origin out of the box and any connector configuration.

Patrick — can you confirm which model your SecOps prefers in principle? If you want, we can run a short workshop next week to walk through the CSR flow and the DNS changes.

Thanks,
Sofia
Sofia Ivanova
Head of Product, Private Deployments
Redwood Inference

Adding the checklist Sofia requested (high level) — happy to expand into a runbook: 

Model A checklist (Delegated FQDN + Redwood edge certs):
- DNS: Acme creates CNAMEs of form <tenant>.acme.redwood.edge -> redwood-edge-<region>.redwood.ai (TTL <= 300 during cutover)
- IP allowlist: Provide Redwood edge egress CIDRs for firewall rules to allow health checks/backends
- Cert ops: Redwood issues and rotates edge certs via public CA. Provide emergency key rotation SLA (we commit 60m for P1).
- Audit: Redwood will publish TLS termination logs to the shared audit bucket (s3) and provide per-request trace ids.

Model B checklist (Split-horizon + origin termination):
- DNS: Acme controls public DNS; internal VPC DNS resolves <tenant>.api.acme.internal -> private runtime IPs.
- CA: Acme must front origin certs signed by an internal CA or public CA. Provide CA root bundle if private CA in PEM.
- mTLS: Redwood runtime supports client certs for mTLS; certs must include SANs matching internal hostnames.
- Rotation: Recommend 90-day rotation cadence with automated CSR flow (we can provide CSR generator). If rotation windows exceed 6 hours, notify Redwood SRE.
- Monitoring: Syslog/JSON push of TLS handshakes and verification results to Acme's SIEM endpoint.

Model C checklist (CSR-proxy hybrid):
- CA exchange: Secure transfer (SFTP or signed envelope) of Acme CA bundle and an audit hash.
- CSR wire: Define JSON schema for CSRs and provisioning responses (we'll share an example).
- Validation: Redwood will validate origin certs against the provided CA bundle and enforce pinning period (default 24 hours).
- Failure modes: If origin cert validation fails, Redwood will fail-closed and route to an outage page; fallback to Redwood-hosted model only if Acme toggles a disaster recovery flag.

I'll open SUP-2345 with these checklists attached. For immediate prototyping, Model C gives a good balance — allows Redwood feature parity while keeping Acme PKI control.

Jonas
Senior Infra Engineer, Redwood Inference

Team / Patrick — thanks for the clear options. From an enablement + risk perspective I approve pursuing Model C (CSR-proxy hybrid) as the default for the Acme pilot, subject to these conditions:

1) Security handshake: Acme provides CA bundle and an L1 contact. We will record a hash of the bundle to the SUP ticket and run validation steps during onboarding.
2) Rotation SLA: Acme commits to a 48-hour notice for planned rotations > 6 hours, Redwood commits to a fallback policy and a documented outage page during any unplanned cert mismatch.
3) Audit & evidence: Redwood will stream TLS-termination logs and validation events to the shared audit bucket with 90-day retention for the pilot.

Action items:
- Patrick: confirm transfer method for CA bundle (SFTP or signed GCS link) and preferred rotation window.
- Karthik: confirm mTLS connector configuration steps and provide a sample config by EOD Monday.
- Jonas: attach the SUP-2345 checklist and the CSR JSON schema to the ticket.
- Sofia: schedule a 60-minute onboarding workshop with Acme SecOps next week — please propose two slots.

If we get all confirmations by Monday EOD, we'll start the pilot onboarding next Wednesday.

Marissa Cole
Director, Private Deployments
Redwood Inference
